references.text: Aron lifted his hands toward the people and blessed them – the priestly blessing by lifting the hands, as Jesus does with the disciples in [ref:3 Mos 9:22|Leviticus 9:22].
Bethany is mentioned as the place near Jerusalem where Jesus had connections, cf. [ref:Luk 19:29|Luke 19:29], where Jesus approaches Bethany and the Mount of Olives.
The following verse [ref:Luk 24:51|Luke 24:51] describes how Jesus was parted from them and taken up into heaven – the ascension that follows directly after the blessing.
Acts gives a parallel account of Jesus' ascension at the Mount of Olives near Bethany, see [ref:Apg 1:9-12|Acts 1:9-12].
Bethany is also mentioned in [ref:Mark 11:1|Mark 11:1] as the place near the Mount of Olives and was an important location in Jesus' ministry.
The Aaronic blessing in [ref:4 Mos 6:23-27|Numbers 6:23-27] is the background for the priestly act of blessing the people, just as Jesus blesses the disciples as the true high priest.

Zechariah could not bless the people after his temple experience ([ref:Luk 1:22|Luke 1:22]). In contrast, Jesus completes the blessing that Zechariah could not give – a theological framework in Luke's Gospel.
Jacob blessed his descendants by laying hands on them ([ref:1 Mos 48:14-15|Genesis 48:14-15]), a parallel to Jesus who lifts his hands to bless the disciples as his spiritual descendants.

Sirach/Ben Sira describes the high priest Simon as blessing the people (non-canonical), but Paul refers to the blessing from Christ in [ref:Ef 1:2|Ephesians 1:2], which can be seen in light of the blessing Jesus gives here.
The Letter to the Hebrews describes Jesus as the eternal high priest who always lives to intercede ([ref:Heb 7:24-25|Hebrews 7:24-25]), a role reflected in his priestly blessing of the disciples.
